build.checks: the model compiles; every #guard of the facts, counterexamples and examples holds; every proof is checked by Lean's kernel; the axiom audit passes
howChecked: lake build checks every proof. The build fails if any proof is wrong or missing.

The Audit library runs #assert_standard_axioms on every theorem named below (61 about TDH, 30 about P53). It fails the build unless the theorem depends only on Lean's three standard axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). A sorry fails it, and so does native_decide, which trusts the compiler.

The same library audits the whole model (Audit/All.lean): every theorem and every definition of every module of the model, the P53 models and the vector runner (1,153 theorems and 1,584 definitions, generated ones included) depends only on those three axioms, and none of those modules declares an axiom or an opaque constant. The runner's JSON parser is written without partial so that the audit covers it too.

Counterexamples and examples are checked at every build too. Some are theorems proved in the kernel by decide. The rest are #guard evaluations of the model, which trust Lean's compiler, as the checks of P26's stated facts in Tdh/Facts.lean do.

Lean 4.35.0, no dependencies. The 6529chain workflow .github/workflows/tdh-formal.yml runs the build, the audit, the vectors and both references on every change to them or to P26, and fails if the committed proof manifest (proof-manifest.json) is not the one the tree gives.

sections.title: Netting invariance
sections.asked: Netting invariance (D131): the result depends only on each transaction's net movements; adding an out-and-back pair or reordering movements inside a transaction changes no output
sections.result: Proved for the stacks only, for two canonical sequences whose transactions correspond one to one and in order, each pair with one timestamp and one txHash (which §3.2 requires) and the same net movements, whenever both replays have a result. Adding or removing a whole transaction, even one whose every net movement is zero, is not covered, and no theorem here goes from a cycle input through the canonical sort to the replay. False for the other values, a record's balance and raw included: §5's mint facts read the logged steps, so a mint and its burn inside one transaction can make a token eligible and give a wallet a balance it did not have (counterexample I), and can change rates and other holders' finals (counterexamples H and I). A token's balance and raw stay the same while its eligibility does; that follows from §7.2's definitions and is not a theorem here. P26 §7.1 states the property for the stacks (1c69528). False for every value under the first rule (fe8e1fe): five counterexamples
sections.guarantees: What it guarantees. Every acquisition stack after the replay, a sink's included, is fixed by each transaction's net movements, transaction by transaction. The assumptions are exactly the theorems' hypotheses: both replays have a result (an inserted step can make the underflow test fail, below), every transaction has one timestamp and one txHash (P26 §3.2 requires it, and checkNetting checks it), the two inputs' transactions correspond one to one and in order, and both replays use one registry and one cluster map (the clusters come from delegation events, which transfers do not change).
sections.limits: What it does not cover. The correspondence is one to one and in order, so an input with one more transaction than another is not covered, even when every net movement of the added transaction is zero; nor is a reordering of whole transactions, which changes the canonical order and can change the stacks, as it should. The theorems start from transfers already in canonical order: no theorem here goes from a cycle input through the canonical sort (§3.3, canonicalTransfers) to the replay, so the property is proved for the replay of two canonical sequences, not for two cycle inputs. What is false: the values beyond the stacks (counterexamples H and I, Tdh/Proofs/Counterexamples.lean). §5's mint facts (firstMint, minted, G, Nc) count every mint as logged, before netting (P26 §5, vector 40). Case H: Meme 1 has 10 copies minted to A and Meme 2 has 5 minted to B; a transaction sends one copy of Meme 1 from A to C. Inserting ZERO -> X and X -> ZERO of 10 copies of Meme 1 into that transaction leaves every net(w) and every pair unchanged, so every stack is the same. But minted[1] rises from 10 to 20, H from 10 to 20, Meme 2's rate from 2.00 to 4.00, and B's final from 800 to 1,600 (the total from 1,710 to 2,510). Such a mint can also set an earlier firstMint, and change eligibility, n_memes and the seasons. Eligibility decides which tokens a record holds at all (§7.2), so it changes balances and raws too. Case I: Meme 2 has 3 copies minted to B ten days before T, so Meme 2 is the only eligible Meme, H is 3, B holds a full set and its final is 32; Meme 1 has 5 copies minted to A an hour before T, so Meme 1 is not eligible and A has no record. Inserting ZERO -> X and X -> ZERO of one copy of Meme 1 into the transaction of Meme 2's mint leaves every net(w), every pair and every stack unchanged, but Meme 1's firstMint moves to ten days before T and its edition is 6. Meme 1 becomes eligible: A has a record with balance 5 (raw 0, held under a day), H rises from 3 to 6, and B, who no longer holds a full set, goes from 32 to 60. With 2 or 10 copies inserted, H is 7 or 15 and B's final 70 or 150, as P26 §7.1 says (it names the other holder Y). So the property cannot be stated for computeCycle's values, a record's balance and raw included; what holds is the stack theorem above, and the values are functions of the stacks and of §5's results. For a token whose eligibility stays the same, its balance and raw are read from its stacks and T (tokenValues), so they stay the same; that is §7.2's definition, and is not a theorem here. Also outside the property, as P26 says. The underflow test decides whether an input is valid, so an inserted step that spends a copy before it arrives makes the input invalid (vector 44). The theorems assume one timestamp and one txHash per transaction; P26 §3.2 makes any other input invalid, and the model checks it (checkNetting).

sections.title: Conservation
sections.asked: Conservation: stack size equals balance; balances never negative under valid inputs; copies held add up to minted minus burned
sections.result: First two proved, with and without netting. The third is false when a sink sends: what holds is held = copies from sinks minus copies to sinks
sections.limits: What is false. "Copies held add up to minted minus burned." A transfer from DEAD credits its recipient with a fresh copy and is not a mint (§3.4). Case G: one copy minted, one sent by DEAD, two held. The inflow counts transfers from every sink: mints from ZERO, and sends from DEAD. What it does not cover. A sink's stack is not a balance: sinks are credit-only. The ages in a stack do change with netting; that is netting's purpose.

sections.title: Totals and identity records
sections.asked: Totals: total TDH equals the sum of identity TDH, which equals the sum of wallet TDH
sections.result: The first holds by definition (computeCycle_totals restates how cycleTotals sums; with the 2^53 range). The second is false for finals: a counterexample. Proved instead: for every identity record there is a list of its wallets, each once, exactly the wallet records with its key, and the identity's balance, raw and base, in total and per token, are the sums over those wallet records; every wallet record belongs to exactly one identity
sections.limits: What it does not cover. The theorem is about the list of wallet records that exists for each identity. It does not prove that the identity record's own wallets field, which the model fills with the members of the identity's cluster (§6.3), is that list. What is false. "The sum of identity TDH equals the sum of wallet TDH." An identity's boost is computed on its own holdings and each token's final is rounded once for the identity (§7.3, §8.4). Case F: two wallets of one identity each hold one Gradient for 100 days. Each wallet record has boost 1.02 and final 102; the identity has boost 1.04 and final 208. The total is 208, not 204. P26 §7.3 now says so, with this example.

sections.title: Order
sections.asked: Order: any permutation of the input list with the same canonical sort gives the same output
sections.result: Proved, for the decoded inputs (any permutation of the transfers, of the delegation events and of the ignored logs' positions, including §3.1's position checks and one-log rule and §3.2's types) and for the raw logs (any permutation of the raw logs and of the decoded items gives the same result, or no result for both), with the header and claims maps taken as fixed. Also proved: in the canonical transfers, any two at one log position share its contract, from and to
sections.guarantees: What it guarantees. The order in which the raw logs and the decoded items arrive cannot matter. When two transfers share a canonical key, or two items of different logs share a (block, logIndex), an ignored log among them, the input is invalid (§3.1), and on decoded inputs the error names the first clash in sorted order, which is the same for every order.
sections.limits: What it does not cover. When several raw logs are malformed, which one the error names can depend on their order (decodeLogs decodes the selected logs in input order), so computeCycleFromSource_perm compares results, not error messages. A transfer's position fields are part of the input: changing them changes the canonical order, as it should. The theorems take the header map and the claims map as fixed: decode_perm and computeCycleFromSource_perm assume that both sources have the same headers (block number to header timestamp) and the same claimTotalMax, and computeCycle_perm and checkInputTypes_perm keep the claims. How a reader builds those maps from JSON (each key the canonical decimal of its integer, no member named twice, so that no two keys name one block or one Meme) is outside them: P26 §3.2's "Values written in JSON" says it, and the vector reader implements it (section 6).

sections.title: Liveness, the cap and the slices
sections.asked: P53 §6.3-§6.4: no capped party exceeds 19.99% of W; slices sum exactly
sections.result: Proved, and stronger: no party at all exceeds 19.99%; the loop stops within six passes, with at most five capped. The proof needs every party's accounts to keep a valid key, which P53 §6.2 now makes part of liveness; for live parties it holds with no assumption on keys. The keys left after the no-pool rule and the lease are inputs of the model, not proved, and the cap needs at least six parties of positive weight
sections.limits: What it does not cover. Membership of designated groups, the lease (the vote in N-7 to N) and key validity are inputs here; the no-pool rule is modelled only for the example. With fewer than six parties there is no cap (CAP_INACTIVE), and the theorems say nothing.

sections.title: Incidents and exclusions
sections.asked: P53 §13.1: no evidence shortens an exclusion in force; evidence for cycles before the end of an earlier exclusion never opens a new incident
sections.result: Proved for a node that keeps incident records, each with the step and length fixed when it opened, which P53 §13.1 now prescribes; pruning records on P53's schedule changes no exclusion. False for a node that recomputes incidents from the evidence it holds: a counterexample
sections.limits: What it does not cover. Joining nodes that read timing from certificates, differences between nodes' views, which account a fault belongs to, the attribution of a fault naming the current cycle "once that cycle's window closes" (the model lets a fault's proof cycle be any cycle at or after the one it names), and the voiding of votes.

sections.title: Raw logs, the boundary and typed inputs
sections.asked: The model from raw logs: selection, decoding, header order and typed inputs as definitions of the model, the decoded-input model as its special case
sections.result: Proved: the model on decoded inputs is the model on raw logs when no log is raw, and a cycle with a result has every input value at its type. The rules themselves (§3.1, §3.2, §4.2, §6.1, §10's types) are definitions, checked by P26's vectors 13, 15, 25-27, 34, 42, 52-55, 61-64, 67-88 and 98-100 and by #guard
sections.limits: What it does not cover. The rules of §3.1, §3.2, §4.2, §5.2's type, §6.1 and §10's types are definitions, not theorems: that they say what P26 says is checked by P26's vectors 13, 15, 25-27, 34, 42, 52-55, 61-64, 67-88 and 98-100, the 2026-10-11 cycle from its 414,254 raw logs, and random inputs against the Python reference, not proved. The vector runner's JSON reading is test tooling and is not proved: TdhVectors/Json.lean parses each file strictly (a text that is not JSON, or an object that names a member twice, is no vector; a number with a fraction or an exponent, or -0, is no integer), TdhVectors/Format.lean checks the whole file's format before any value is read, and TdhVectors/Input.lean maps each value to the model's without cutting any and refuses a JSON value of the wrong kind (a string for an integer, whatever it spells; a map key that is not the canonical decimal of its integer; a removed that is not a boolean). These are the rules of how values are written in JSON, and they stay outside the model's boundary, where P26's prose governs them (the proposal, below). A node's own reads stay outside the model too: which chain is canonical and finalized, that its log set is complete for [deployment, B] (§3.1), the headers its search for B reads (§4.2), and totalMax at B (§5.2, P27 §5).

sections.title: Clusters and the four-wallet gate
sections.asked: Clusters (D136): no cluster larger than the registry allows, its wallets pairwise confirmed, a fourth wallet only through the gate; registrations before activation never form a group of four
sections.result: Proved, for every cycle with a result: every cluster holds at most consolidation_max_wallets distinct wallets, any two with a confirmed row, and past consolidation_ungated_max_wallets a member whose rows with all the others were registered both ways at or after the activation time; on a cycle whose T is before it, no cluster has more than consolidation_ungated_max_wallets wallets. Which of several possible clusters the greedy order picks is P26's vectors' to pin, not a theorem
sections.guarantees: What it guarantees. No cycle result holds a cluster larger than its registry allows, a cluster with two wallets that have no confirmed link, or a cluster past the ungated size without a member whose links with all the others are fresh, whatever the events and their times; and no cycle before the activation time has a cluster of more than three wallets under tdh-v1.4.
sections.limits: What it does not cover. The theorems are about which wallets may share a cluster, not about which of several possible clusters the greedy order picks: that is the order of §6.3's queue (newest block first, then ascending pair key), which P26's vectors 89-99 pin, and which P26 §6.3 reports equal to 6529.io's own code on 100,000 random link graphs. That pairKey's string order is the order of the sorted pairs of addresses is checked by #guard on examples (Tdh/Facts.lean), not proved. That §6.2 and §6.3 are 6529.io's planConsolidationEvent and extractConsolidations is a statement about P26's text, which the vectors and the references' runs test; no theorem here relates the model to 6529.io's code.

sections.title: The acquisition stack
sections.limits: These theorems are about how the model stores a stack: they show that it behaves as P26 §7.1's list. Which entries the replay pushes and takes is the subject of sections 1 and 2.
sections.guarantees: The first proofs about the model. They show that the run-length stack of Tdh.Stack is exactly P26 §7.1's "ordered list of acquisition timestamps": push appends at the end, takeLast removes exactly the last amount entries and returns them in order, it fails exactly when the list is shorter (the input is then invalid), and size is the list's length. Everything the model computes from stacks therefore follows P26's list semantics.

theorems.claim: Total TDH equals the sum of wallet TDH
theorems.statement: Total TDH is not the sum of wallet TDH. Identity {A, B}; each wallet holds one Gradient for 100 days. Each wallet record has one Gradient (boost 1.02, final 102); the identity holds two (boost 1.04, final 208). The total is the identity's, 208, not 204.

theorems.claim: Copies held add up to minted minus burned
theorems.statement: Copies held are not minted minus burned. A transfer from DEAD credits its recipient with a fresh copy and is not a mint (§3.4). One Meme is minted to B, and DEAD sends a copy to A: two copies are held, one was minted, none was burned. What holds is held = inflow - outflow (held_eq_inflow_sub_outflow), where the inflow counts transfers from every sink: from ZERO and from DEAD.

theorems.claim: Steps that leave every net(w) unchanged change no value" (P26 §7.1 before 2026-10-15)
theorems.statement: A mint and its burn change values, with every net movement unchanged. Until 2026-10-15 P26 §7.1's property said that steps leaving every net(w) unchanged change no value. They change no stack (net_invariance), but §5's mint facts read the logged steps. Meme 1 has 10 copies minted to A and Meme 2 has 5 minted to B; a transaction sends one copy of Meme 1 from A to C. Inserting ZERO -> X and X -> ZERO of 10 copies of Meme 1 into that transaction leaves every net(w) and every pair unchanged, but minted[1] rises from 10 to 20, so H doubles, Meme 2's rate doubles from 2.00 to 4.00, and B's final goes from 800 to 1,600.

Checked by evaluating the model at build time (#guard), which trusts Lean's compiler; it is not a proof checked by the kernel.

theorems.claim: Such steps change no stack, balance or raw" (P26 §7.1 after H, until round 3 of 2026-10-15)
theorems.statement: A mint and its burn change a balance, with every stack unchanged. After case H, P26 §7.1 said that such steps change no stack, balance or raw. Only the stacks are proved (replayHoldings_invariance): a record holds a token's balance and raw only while the token is eligible (§7.2, walletTokens), and eligibility reads §5's mint facts. Meme 2 has 3 copies minted to B ten days before T; Meme 1 has 5 copies minted to A an hour before T, so Meme 1 is not eligible and A has no record. Inserting ZERO -> X and X -> ZERO of one copy of Meme 1 into the transaction of Meme 2's mint leaves every net(w), every pair and so every stack as it was, but moves Meme 1's firstMint to ten days before T. Meme 1 becomes eligible: A has a record with balance 5 (raw 0, held under a day), H rises from 3 to 6, and B, who no longer holds a full set, goes from 32 to 60. With 2 or 10 copies inserted, H is 7 or 15 and B's final 70 or 150. P26 §7.1 gives this example, with the other holder named Y, since round 3 of 2026-10-15, and states the property for the stacks; a token's balance and raw stay the same only while its eligibility does.
